about: Every capability: the CLI command and the MCP tool that provide it, and the operation both of them run. `cli` is the command path without the binary; `mcp` is a tool name; `operation` is the function exported from packages/<package>/src/operations (or the core's) that both reach — a list when the command is several. `argv` and `args` are what the check adds to the command and the tool to get there — and what tells apart two rows of one command and one tool, `update --later` from `update --auto off` — `via` another row's operation a side passes through first, `expect` what the operation must receive from both sides, by parameter name (`null` for not given) — needed where another row runs the same operation through another command and another tool, so the two cannot be swapped unnoticed — and `unchecked` says why a row is not checked, instead of `operation`. Checked by test/parity.test.mjs in `pnpm verify` against both registries, read from the running product, and by running each row's command and tool with every operation replaced by a stand-in that records the call and its arguments; `pnpm verify:parity --strict`, also part of `pnpm verify`, refuses any pending row. How to add one: CONTRIBUTING.md, "Adding a capability". Design: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-25-cli-mcp-parity-design.md.

capabilities.reason: Every agent session on this machine, every project and account among them, is the person's view — the CLI's and the desktop app's through it. An MCP tool that listed them would hand one project's mail subjects to another project's agent, so over MCP comms_activity answers only for the session it is called from (design 2026-10-25-activity S3).

Any session's calls, by its key, is the person's view. Over MCP no argument names a session: comms_activity shows the calling session's own, worked out by the server itself, so an agent cannot read another window's subjects and senders by guessing or copying a key (design 2026-10-25-activity S3).

Every session's calls that name an item, grouped by the item — which window read a message, replied to it or posted in its thread — is the person's view, the CLI's and the desktop app's through it, and is refused inside an MCP server's process. A tool that answered it would hand one project's mail subjects and senders to another project's agent; over MCP comms_activity answers only for the calling window (design 2026-10-25-activity S3; 2026-10-26-owner-feedback-0320 §3.6, §4).

The calling session's own calls and counts: an MCP server answers for the agent window that started it, a command for the window it runs in or for itself alone — the session read from the process, never from an argument (design 2026-10-25-activity S3).
Recording off applies at once; recording again is a loosening the person approves (design 2026-10-25-activity §4.1).
Fewer days kept applies at once and deletes the older days; more days is a loosening the person approves (design 2026-10-25-activity §4.1).

Where Search on this machine stands — on or off, the accounts, counts, size, the oldest day, the model's state, backups and FileVault — is content-free and is shown by doctor, so comms_doctor gives an agent the same facts; a tool of its own would add nothing an agent needs (design 2026-10-26-local-search §7, §8).

What everyone asked, across every kept account, searchable by meaning, is the widest read there is: the person's alone, in the app and at a terminal, refused inside an MCP server's process and under an agent's marker. No MCP tool returns message content (2026-10-26-owner-feedback-0320 §4); agents search each account live with gmail_search and slack_search (design 2026-10-26-local-search S13).

Every person a message is kept from, with their addresses and Slack users, across every account, is the person's view, refused inside an MCP server's process and under an agent's marker; a tool would hand one project's correspondents to another project's agent (design 2026-10-26-local-search S5, S13).
What one person sent, across every kept account, is the person's read, refused inside an MCP server's process and under an agent's marker, as search query is (design 2026-10-26-local-search S13).

A kept message in full is message content from the person's own store, refused inside an MCP server's process and under an agent's marker; agents read a message live, through their own recorded read (design 2026-10-26-local-search S13).

The indexer is the one writer of the person's search database, run by the person's own commands and the app — never as a job of its own and never by an agent; refused inside an MCP server's process and under an agent's marker (design 2026-10-26-local-search S8, S10, S13).

Making every vector again from the kept text is upkeep of the person's own store, refused inside an MCP server's process and under an agent's marker, as search index is (design 2026-10-26-local-search §5, S13).

Joining two people is the person's own act: names never join, and no agent may decide that two handles are one person; refused inside an MCP server's process and under an agent's marker (design 2026-10-26-local-search S5, S13).
Separating a handle from a person undoes the person's own join, and is theirs alone, as search link is (design 2026-10-26-local-search S5, S13).

The name the person knows someone by is kept sealed in the person's own store and is theirs to give; refused inside an MCP server's process and under an agent's marker (design 2026-10-26-local-search S5, S11, S13).

Switching Search on is the first store whose job is to keep message words: a loosening the person approves — at a terminal, or in the attested app with --app-approval — and refused inside an MCP server's process and under an agent's marker, so no tool can ask for it (design 2026-10-26-local-search S1, S13).

Off is a tightening that applies at once from anywhere; a tool for it alone would let an agent stop what the person chose to keep, which only the person, in the app or at a terminal, decides (design 2026-10-26-local-search S1, §8).

Keeping one more account's messages is a loosening the person approves, at a terminal or in the attested app, and refused inside an MCP server's process and under an agent's marker (design 2026-10-26-local-search S1, S2, S13).

Taking an account out applies at once from anywhere and deletes what is kept of it; it is the person's setting, changed in the app or at a terminal, with no tool (design 2026-10-26-local-search §7, §8).

Sending kept words to a local model server, even on loopback, is a loosening the person approves, at a terminal or in the attested app; refused inside an MCP server's process and under an agent's marker (design 2026-10-26-local-search S9, S13).
Words only applies at once from anywhere and drops every vector; the person's setting, with no tool (design 2026-10-26-local-search S9, §8).

Delete everything is a tightening that applies at once from anywhere once --all --confirm says so — or the app's confirm — and deletes the key with the folder; a tool would put an irreversible delete of the person's store one agent call away (design 2026-10-26-local-search §7).
Which files may be attached: the folders they may come from, the person's own deny entries, and the built-in list. `comms_attach` with no change is this report.
A folder added widens what can be attached, so it is a change the person approves; the preview says where a link leads.
A folder taken away narrows what can be attached, and applies at once.
A deny entry added narrows what can be attached, and applies at once.
A deny entry taken away widens what can be attached, so it is a change the person approves; the built-in list cannot be removed.
How what an agent sends is labelled: the word, the name, every rule, and who each kind of message on each account appears to come from. `comms_label` with no change is this report.
A new word changes how the label looks, so it is a change the person approves; the preview shows the phrase recipients will see.
A new name changes how the label looks, so it is a change the person approves; `--clear` and `name: null` take it away the same way.
A rule `as: me` sends a kind of message unlabelled, so it is approved first; a rule `as: agent` labels more and applies at once.
Removing an `agent` rule can leave a message unlabelled, so it is approved first; removing a `me` rule labels more and applies at once.
The icon of the app's Slack posts changes how the label looks, so it is a change the person approves; `--clear` and `emoji: null` go back to the person's photo the same way.
A Slack workspace's style `labelled` trades Slack's own APP tag, which no one can fake, for words in the message, so it is a change the person approves; `app`, the default, applies at once.

What an agent may do: every rule, whether its account is still connected, and what each account allows, across it and in each conversation a rule names. `comms_behaviour` with no change is this report.
A rule that lets an agent do more anywhere — an act added, a conversation allowed more than its account — is a change the person approves; one that only narrows what is allowed applies at once.
Removing a rule lets the wider one hold there, so it is approved first, unless that one allows no more.

Taking messages, per account: whether a session must take a message before it acts on it, what a take says to the sender, and when a message nobody took counts. `comms_taking` with no change is this report.
Requiring a take applies at once; letting sessions act without taking a message first is a loosening the person approves (design 2026-10-26-taking-messages §5).
Saying nothing to the sender applies at once; a 👀 on taking is a loosening the person approves, made only under a standing approval they made at their terminal (§7).
When a message nobody took counts as not taken only decides when the person hears of it, so it applies at once either way.
Whether the person is reminded of a message nobody took applies at once either way: it waits under Not taken regardless.

Every session's takes, offers, hand-backs and notes — their folders and clients among them — is the person's view, the CLI's and the desktop app's through it, and is refused inside an MCP server's process and in an agent's shell. A tool that answered it would name one project's agent to another's, and hand on notes an agent may have copied a sender's words into; over MCP each channel's `*_taken` answers in closed words only (design 2026-10-26-taking-messages T7, T8, §5).

Ending a take is the person's override: no session may end another's (design 2026-10-26-taking-messages §2, §10), and a session's own hand-back is its channel's take tool with `step: "hand-back"`. Refused inside an MCP server's process and in an agent's shell.

Giving a message to a window is the person's: no session may offer a message to another, or to itself past another's take (§2, T4, §10). Refused inside an MCP server's process and in an agent's shell.

Keeping a message is the person saying they will handle it, which refuses every session; a session takes for itself only, with its channel's take tool (T2, §10). Refused inside an MCP server's process and in an agent's shell.

What an agent may send without asking: each standing approval's contents by digest, places, limits and end, its uses in the last day and its last 10 acts. `comms_standing` with no change is this report (design 2026-10-19-standing-approvals, S10).

A narrowing keeps fewer contents or places, lowers a limit or ends it sooner, so it applies at once and asks nobody; one that would allow more is refused, naming Slack's standing add, which a person approves at a terminal (S8, §8.2).
Ending one standing approval, and every unused act of it, only takes away, so it applies at once and asks nobody (S8, §8.5).
Ending every standing approval at once raises the standing epoch each record and each unused act is bound to, so loosening anything later revives none; it only takes away, so it asks nobody (S8).

The writing profile for one place — the account and its conversations — and every file it would read, which an agent reads before it writes there. It only reads, and needs no approval (design 2026-10-19-agent-behaviour-rules, B6).

A writing profile is the person's own instructions to their agents: a tool that wrote one would let something an agent read change how every later message is written. So only the person starts one, at a terminal, from a starter that never overwrites a file; over MCP comms_profile only reads (design 2026-10-19-agent-behaviour-rules, B6).
Adding an organisation's profile — its Google client and Slack apps, beside what is here — is a change the person approves, bound to the profile's SHA-256 (design 2026-10-02 §D5).

Reading a profile again: a changed profile, a new source, a looser update cap and serving other addresses are approved first; repairing drift, a tighter update cap and turning other addresses off apply at once (design 2026-10-02 §D8, 2026-10-19 X6).
Forgetting a profile deletes the clients it made, with their secrets, and cannot be taken back: approved first, bound to the rows it removes (design 2026-10-02 §D8).

One change for every step: each registration registered again at the latest release with its own name, client, scope, launcher and pins, the runtimes that needs, and the global packages. `update --check` and `check: true` are `updateCheck`, the read both sides run instead, which asks nobody.
How this machine updates — auto, every-14-days or never — in config.json: a level that updates less is a loosening the person approves, one that updates more applies at once (design 2026-10-16, U2).
Holds every update notice on this machine for 1, 7 or 14 days, 7 by default: a plain answer with no approval, since nothing is stopped any more, and never for a security fix (design 2026-10-16, U3).
Ends a pause at once, with no approval (design 2026-10-16, U3).

Back to the release before: every stable launcher's pointer switched back to the runtime it started before its last switch — a change the person approves, one effect a launcher, which edits no client configuration (design 2026-10-16, U6).

Setting up the per-user job that installs verified releases in the background: an effect the person approves, its preview naming the job file and what it runs, when it runs, what macOS shows and how to remove it (design 2026-10-16 U4).
Removing the background update job: it only makes this machine do less, so it applies at once and takes no approval (design 2026-10-16 U4).

One background run, as the per-user job starts it once a day with no terminal and no agent: a verified release past its hold, installed, checked and switched to; --dry-run only says what it would do. It is the job's entry, not a tool: an agent in a conversation updates with comms_update, whose preview a person approves, and this run exists so that no conversation waits for an update (design 2026-10-16 U4, U5).
Where updates stand here, read from local files, asking npm nothing (desktop design DA13).

Approving a change under the `confirm` change policy means a person at a terminal typing the code shown; a tool that approved would make `confirm` mean nothing (design §6.3). Under `chat` there is nothing to approve from a tool: the tool that prepared the change applies it when called again with the approval id, after the person's yes.
It runs the MCP server. A tool is a call into a server that is already running, so no tool can be the one that starts it.
`agentcomms mcp install` registers the core server; comms_server_install registers any channel's, and with `channel: "core"` is this command.

Several servers for one client as one change (design 2026-10-26-desktop-0340, B3): `agentcomms mcp install --server <a,b,…>` and comms_server_install with `servers` run the same operation — one plan, one preview naming every server, one approval, each registered in order, the first failure stopping the rest. One server stays the single-install row's operation.

`agentcomms mcp prune` with no `--server` prunes every managed server's runtimes, listed by server; comms_server_prune with no `channel` is this command. Each passes no server to the shared prune operation, which takes every server the channel registry declares.
`agentcomms mcp prune --server core` prunes the core's own runtimes; comms_server_prune with `channel: "core"` is this command.
The service declaration makes `events` a managed server; the core command and tool pass that same declared server id to the shared registration operation.
The service declaration makes `events` a managed server; the core command and tool pass that same declared server id to the shared prune operation.

`agentcomms mcp uninstall --client <c> --server <s>` takes one server out of one client's configuration, and comms_server_uninstall with `channel` and `client` is this command: a tightening, applied at once with no approval (design 2026-10-26-owner-feedback-0320 §3.3, §4). Prune is not this — it removes runtimes, and no registration.
A change approval on both surfaces. The tool reads the client JSON from a path on this machine, so the file never passes through the conversation, and neither side returns the secret.

after.serverInstallChange: A sign-in `setup --mcp-client` handed off carries the client it was asked to register with, and `inbox add --finish` registers it once the mailbox is connected — through the change `mcp install` runs, approved the same way. gmail_inbox_finish does not: this server has no tool that registers anything, so it returns the registration as `pendingRegistration`, naming the core server's comms_server_install with `channel: "gmail"`, that client, `inbox` — the mailbox just connected — when the entry under that name serves another, `name: "gmail-<org>"` — a second entry of its own — when that entry serves another and is not being replaced, and `force` when `setup` was given `--replace-server` — the same change, from chat (design §5). Both decide by the same rule that the client already has it: an entry of ours under that name, at user scope, unpinned or pinned to this mailbox, whose runtime is there (`clientServesInbox`).

capabilities.reason: The CLI completes a sign-in begun with --start as `inbox add --finish <flowId>`. Over MCP that is a call of its own, because a tool call cannot sit waiting on a browser.
Asking for more than the mailbox holds is a change approval, given before the sign-in link exists; renewing or narrowing starts at once.
The CLI completes a re-authorisation as `inbox reauth --finish <flowId>`. Over MCP gmail_inbox_finish finishes either kind of sign-in, because a tool call cannot sit waiting on a browser.

Both directions, for the send policy and the change policy. Tightening applies at once; loosening is a change approval on either surface (design §3). One row, since what was the loosening row now names the same command and tool.

The first call of a download: it saves nothing, and answers with the question where to save — Downloads, the current folder, or a folder the person names — and a choice id. The command, run by an agent or with no terminal, exits 10 with the same question.

The same download, answered: the person's answer and the question's id — `--to` and `--choice` on the command, `saveTo` and `choiceId` on the tool — reach the operation alike, which claims the question and saves.
The command reads the body from `--text`, `--file <path>` or standard input (`--file -`); the tool takes it as `text`, the chat's way to pass prose that no shell has to quote.
The command reads the body from `--text`, `--file <path>` or standard input (`--file -`); the tool takes it as `text`, the chat's way to pass prose that no shell has to quote.
A new body comes from `--text` or `--file` (`--file -` for standard input) at a terminal, and from `text` in chat; given none, both keep the body the draft has.

Approving under the `confirm` policy means a person at a terminal typing the code shown (design §6.3). A tool that approved would make `confirm` mean nothing; over MCP the answer is the command to run.
Both refuse a client without a recent probe, then ask for a change approval: the probe is the evidence, the approval the decision.

It tests the MCP client's own approval form by raising one, so a person can see it reaches them. A terminal has no form to test; what the probe shows is then recorded with gmail_confirm_client_add or `confirm-clients add`.

This session takes a message before it replies, so no other session does (design 2026-10-26-taking-messages §5). The session is the server's or the command's own, never an argument; at the person's own terminal a command takes nothing.
The holder hands a message back with a closed reason other sessions see, and a note for the person alone (T8).
The holder marks a message done; other sessions stay refused it (T3).
Who has these messages, in closed words — never another session's folder, client or key (T7); with none named, this session's own takes.
It runs the MCP server. A tool is a call into a server that is already running, so no tool can be the one that starts it.

From chat this is the core server's comms_server_install, which registers any channel's server: `channel: "gmail"` is this command — the same change, `serverInstallChange`, so an approval either one prepared is claimed by the other (design §5).

From chat this is the core server's comms_server_prune, which prunes any channel's runtimes: `channel: "gmail"` is this command — the same change, `serverPruneChange`, so an approval either one prepared is claimed by the other (design §5).

after.startSignIn: When the named mailbox is not connected yet, setup continues from its state report into the same sign-in that inbox add starts.

capabilities.reason: The report `setup` starts from: the eligible client for the target mailbox, the clients and mailboxes there are, the MCP clients the server is registered with, the downloaded client files, and the one step to take next. With no --profile it changes nothing. The steps `setup` then takes are the rows that follow.

`setup --profile <file>` and gmail_setup profile add the organisation through core's orgAddChange first, under the separate --org-approval/orgApproval, then continue Gmail setup (design 2026-10-02 §D6).

capabilities.unchecked: `setup` registers the client only when `setupState` finds none, and in the drive `setupState` is a stand-in that finds nothing to compare, so `setup --client-json` never reaches the step there. It runs clientAddChange, as `client add` and gmail_client_add do: packages/gmail/test/account-changes.test.ts, "setup --client-json registers the client the same way client add does".
capabilities.reason: `setup --client-json <path>` registers the OAuth client through the change `client add` runs, under the name "desktop"; from chat that step is gmail_client_add.

`setup --inbox <name> [--email]` starts the sign-in `inbox add --start` starts; from chat that step is gmail_inbox_add, finished by gmail_inbox_finish. At a terminal, setup waits for the browser itself.
`setup --mcp-client <client>` registers the server as `mcp install` does; from chat that step is the core server's comms_server_install with `channel: "gmail"` (design §5).

A Resend API key is typed by a person at a terminal, from a hidden prompt or `RESEND_API_KEY` in that terminal: a key typed into a chat stays in the transcript. From chat, the answer is the command to run.
A change approval, because a deleted key cannot be taken back.
Reports, and tightens at once; loosening the send policy, the mode or the change policy is a change approval, under the change policy in force before it — the account's own when it sets one.
Sends once, and only an email a person approved: the claim, the content and the recipients are all checked again before Resend is asked.
One this machine scheduled is cancelled at once; one scheduled elsewhere is a change approval, because a cancelled email cannot be rescheduled.
Approving under the `confirm` policy means a person at a terminal typing the code shown. A tool that approved would make `confirm` mean nothing; over MCP the answer is the command to run.
It runs the MCP server. A tool is a call into a server that is already running, so no tool can be the one that starts it.

From chat this is the core server's comms_server_install, which registers any channel's server: `channel: "resend"` is this command — the same change, `serverInstallChange`, so an approval either one prepared is claimed by the other (design §5). Pinned with the generic `account`, as `--account` here.

From chat this is the core server's comms_server_prune, which prunes any channel's runtimes: `channel: "resend"` is this command — the same change, `serverPruneChange`, so an approval either one prepared is claimed by the other (design §5).

A session takes a received email before it replies to it, so no other session answers it (design 2026-10-26-taking-messages §5): the session is the server's or the command's own, never an argument. `step` tells the take from the hand-back and the done.
Only the holder hands an email back, with a closed reason other sessions see and a note only the person does (T8).
Only the holder marks an email done; other sessions stay refused it (T3).
Who has each received email, in closed words — `you`, `another session`, `the person` — never who another session is (T7); with none named, this session's own.

`workspace add <name>` with no client id chooses the organisation profile's read app, or its send app for `mode: "send"`; an explicit client id and port keep the own-app path. Send is approved before sign-in; read starts at once.
The CLI completes a sign-in begun with --start as `workspace add --finish <flowId>`. Over MCP that is a call of its own, because a tool call cannot sit waiting on a browser.

Changes nothing and starts nothing: returns the steps for a move to send. For a profile account those steps are the move to the profile's send app, which `slack_mode_set` (`workspace mode <name> send`) performs after approval and Slack consent; for an own-app account they are the existing manifest/app-update steps.

Changes nothing and starts nothing: returns the steps for a move to read. For a profile account those steps are the move to the profile's read app, which `slack_mode_set` (`workspace mode <name> read`) performs at once, followed by Slack consent; for an own-app account they are the existing manifest/removal/reauth procedure.

`workspace mode <name> send|read` moves a profile account between the organisation's apps (`send` needs approval; `read` starts at once); an own-app account keeps the existing app-update/removal instructions.
A change approval, because a deleted token cannot be taken back.
Renewing starts at once; read → send is a change approval, given before the sign-in starts.
The CLI completes a sign-in again as `workspace reauth <name> --finish <flowId>`; over MCP the one finishing tool completes every sign-in, bound to the name when it is given.
Reports, and tightens at once; loosening a send or change policy is a change approval, under the change policy in force before it.

The first call of a download: it saves nothing, and answers with the question where to save — Downloads, the current folder, or a folder the person names — and a choice id. The command, run by an agent or with no terminal, exits 10 with the same question.

The same download, answered: the person's answer and the question's id — `--to` and `--choice` on the command, `saveTo` and `choiceId` on the tool — reach the operation alike, which claims the question and saves.
Every file taken off: `--no-files` on the command, `files: []` on the tool — an empty list, which a list of paths cannot say on the command line.
The CLI claims a reaction's approval as `react --approval <id>`. Over MCP that is a call of its own, as posting is.

Prepares a standing approval, reading each place's name, member count and sharing for its preview (design 2026-10-19-standing-approvals, §8.1). Neither side approves it: only the person's code at a terminal does, through `approve`.

Sends one acknowledgement under a standing approval (design 2026-10-19-standing-approvals, S9): the message and a content digest, no draft. Its one-shot child is claimed through the same path as every Slack act.

Approving under the `confirm` policy means a person at a terminal typing the code shown (design §6.3). A tool that approved would make `confirm` mean nothing; over MCP the answer is the command to run.
It runs the MCP server. A tool is a call into a server that is already running, so no tool can be the one that starts it.

From chat this is the core server's comms_server_install, which registers any channel's server: `channel: "slack"` is this command — the same change, `serverInstallChange`, so an approval either one prepared is claimed by the other (design §5).

From chat this is the core server's comms_server_prune, which prunes any channel's runtimes: `channel: "slack"` is this command — the same change, `serverPruneChange`, so an approval either one prepared is claimed by the other (design §5).

Needs an app configuration token, which must never pass through chat: the transcript would keep it. From chat, slack_manifest returns the manifest and the app's manifest page to paste it into (design §4, §6.4).

Takes the send app's bot token at a hidden prompt, from a person at a terminal: an agent never handles a secret, and a token typed into a chat stays in the transcript. From chat the answer is the command for the person to run (design 2026-10-15 S1, revised).
Needs an app configuration token, which must never pass through chat. From chat, slack_manifest returns the manifest to create the app from on api.slack.com (design §4, §6.4).

Takes a message for the session the server or command runs in — never one an argument names — after reading it from Slack to check it is someone else's (design 2026-10-26-taking-messages T2, T5). `slack_take` with no step is a take.
The holder hands a message back, with a closed reason others may see and a note for the person alone (T8): `take --hand-back` at a terminal, `step: "hand-back"` over MCP.
The holder marks a message done, and other sessions stay refused it (T3): `take --done` at a terminal, `step: "done"` over MCP.
Who has each message, in closed words — never which session (T7): reads only this machine's records.
The command can also open the link with `--open`, for a person only; the tool never opens anything and returns the link for the person to click.

Choosing which file on this Mac an agent may read is the person's decision, and the first read of WhatsApp's folder is the moment macOS asks that person for permission, which a server cannot answer. Refused to an agent at the command line too.
The other half of `add`: it forgets the account, the person's chat lists for it and its index. The person's step, refused to an agent at the command line too.

Which chats an agent may see is the person's choice, in both directions: a tool would let an agent widen what it sees. Kept outside `config.json`, where no loosening of it could be judged, and refused to an agent at the command line too.
The other side of `allow`: an agent neither widens nor narrows what later sessions see. The person's list, refused to an agent at the command line too.
It undoes `allow` and `deny`, which are the person's; emptying an allow list shows every chat again, which an agent must not be able to do.

Approving a change under the `confirm` change policy — registering or pruning this server — means a person at a terminal typing the code shown; a tool that approved would make `confirm` mean nothing. There is no send to approve: this package never sends.
It runs the MCP server. A tool is a call into a server that is already running, so no tool can be the one that starts it.

From chat this is the core server's comms_server_install, which registers any channel's server: `channel: "whatsapp"` with `account` is this command with `--account` — the same change, `serverInstallChange`, so an approval either one prepared is claimed by the other (design §5).

From chat this is the core server's comms_server_prune, which prunes any channel's runtimes: `channel: "whatsapp"` is this command — the same change, `serverPruneChange`, so an approval either one prepared is claimed by the other (design §5).

It refuses inside the event service's MCP server, and no tool reads it; events_deliveries_list gives an agent the content-free rows.

Binding a lane lets one agent window read what arrives in it, so it is the person's act at an interactive terminal, where they type the lane's name, or from the app through one: no tool binds, and the command refuses an agent's shell and the event service's MCP server. An agent learns its own window's id with events_lane_whoami and gives it to the person (routing design 2026-10-25, B1).

It says which agent window it is called from, as the event service's MCP server in that window works it out from its Claude Code session id and its activity session. A terminal is no agent window, so there is nothing for a command to say; the person sees every window in the app, from the activity log (routing design 2026-10-25, B1, B6).

It answers with an MCP task that wakes the agent window it was called from when that window's lane has a new item. It means something only to a bound agent window, and a terminal has no window to wake (routing design 2026-10-25, §3.4, §3.7).

It holds the bound agent window's own call until its lane's next item, for at most 50 seconds, for clients without the tasks extension. Only a bound agent window has a lane to wait on; the person sees the queue in the app (routing design 2026-10-25, §3.6, §3.7).

It reads a lane's item for the one agent window the person bound to that lane, and only items that arrived after the binding. The person reads every item, a lane's included, with the queue's own content reads at a terminal or in the app (routing design 2026-10-25, B2, B3, §3.7).

What happened to each message — its deliveries, the queue item it became and that item's history: which agent window was woken for it and read it, and who marked it — is the person's own view, at a terminal or in the app. No MCP tool returns it, so no agent window learns of an item in a lane bound to another (0.32.0 spec §3.6, §4).

Judge setup turns a judge kind on, and the judge budget when it has none for the judge's provider: standing disclosure authorisations, which the command approves as the person's own act. So it is the person's, from the attested desktop app or an interactive terminal: it refuses an agent's shell, the event service's MCP server and, on macOS, a process the app did not start; on Windows and Linux, which attest nothing, it sends the person to their terminal, and no tool performs it (owner decision 2026-10-26; events design D2).
secret material must never enter model input or output; the person completes this operation at the terminal or app.

An AI provider's key is the person's account, kept in the app's Settings → AI providers or at their terminal: removing one is theirs too, and an agent must never ask for, see, set or remove one; no tool does. On Windows and Linux, which attest nothing, setting or removing one is done at the person's terminal (owner decision 2026-10-26).

A workflow's activation is a standing disclosure the person approves: in the Agent Comms app, after its preview, as judge setup's are (0.33.0 design §3.1; events design D2). So it is the person's, from the attested app only: it refuses an agent's shell, the event service's MCP server and, on macOS, a process the app did not start; on Windows and Linux, which attest nothing, it sends the person to their terminal, where they type the challenge with approve, and no tool performs either.

Switching the event service on is a standing disclosure the person approves: in the Agent Comms app, after the preview of what enable-all prepared, as a workflow's activation is (0.34.0 design B4; events design D2). So it is the person's, from the attested app only: it refuses an agent's shell, the event service's MCP server and, on macOS, a process the app did not start; on Windows and Linux, which attest nothing, it sends the person to their terminal, where they type the challenge with approve, and no tool performs either.

Analyse is the person's view of one workflow and what it did on this Mac in the last 30 days — its counts, the judge's answers per sending domain — run when they press it, in the app or at an interactive terminal, on the model provider they picked with their own key. No tool runs it, and the command refuses the event service's MCP server, an agent's shell and, on macOS, a process the app did not start: an agent never reads those counts and never spends the person's key without getting past that speed bump, and only the person applies a suggestion (0.33.0 design §3.3, §3.7).

What Linear shows the person — their workspace, its teams and a team's labels, fetched with their own Linear key — is for the person choosing a Linear target, in the app's Settings → Integrations or at a terminal (0.33.0 design §3.4). No tool reaches it, and the command refuses inside the event service's MCP server and in an agent's shell, by its marker (a speed bump against agents, not a boundary); events_provider_list tells an agent whether a Linear key is kept.

Where Agent Comms finds the person's claude-stream relay — its home folder and its port — is the person's own setting, shown in the app's Settings → Integrations or at their terminal. That folder holds the relay's control token, so an agent cannot read the setting through Agent Comms: no tool shows it, and the command refuses inside the event service's MCP server and in an agent's shell, by its marker (a speed bump against agents, not a boundary) (0.33.0 design §3.5).

Pointing Agent Comms at a relay decides which coding-agent sessions a workflow can prompt, with that relay's control token, so it is the person's, from the attested app or an interactive terminal, as an AI provider's key is, and an agent cannot provide it: the command refuses an agent's shell and the event service's MCP server, sends the person to their terminal on Windows and Linux, which attest nothing, the owner takes it only from the person's origin, and no tool sets it (0.33.0 design §3.5).

A match waiting for a busy agent session is passed on when the session's run ends; dropping one is the person's, in the app or at their terminal, as clearing the queue is: no tool drops one, and the command refuses inside the event service's MCP server and in an agent's shell, by its marker (a speed bump against agents, not a boundary). A bound window sees its own lane's waiting matches with events_session_queue_list (0.33.0 design §3.5).
